claims.text: Intrinsic lattice distortions hinder dislocation motion under dynamic mechanical loading in high-entropy alloys.
Hindered dislocation motion increases strain hardening in high-entropy alloys.
Hindered dislocation motion increases the dynamic strength of high-entropy alloys.
Lattice distortions allow localized alternative deformation mechanisms that preserve ductility.
The proposed material is a single-phase high-entropy alloy with significant lattice distortion arising from atomic-size mismatch.
The controlled comparison uses dynamic mechanical testing above approximately 10^3 s^-1 on the HEA and a conventional single-phase alloy with minimal lattice distortion.
Testing is conducted at room temperature under high-strain-rate loading.
Intrinsic lattice distortions and local chemical disorder affect dislocation mobility.
Severe lattice distortions create a rugged energy landscape for dislocation glide.
The rugged energy landscape impedes dislocation glide and thereby increases strength and strain hardening.
Lattice distortions facilitate localized alternative deformation pathways such as twinning.
Localized alternative deformation pathways allow the HEA to maintain ductility.
Under dynamic loading, the HEA will have higher dynamic strength than the conventional-alloy baseline.
Under dynamic loading, the HEA will have a higher strain-hardening rate than the conventional-alloy baseline.
Under dynamic loading, the HEA will maintain ductility comparable to that of the conventional-alloy baseline.
The proposed mechanism is limited to single-phase HEAs having significant atomic-size-mismatch-induced lattice distortion.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to alloys with multiphase microstructures or extensive secondary phases.
The magnitude of the predicted strength and ductility changes may vary with alloy composition and testing setup.
TEM and XRD characterization can be used to look for dislocation structures, inhibited dislocation motion, and alternative deformation mechanisms such as twinning after dynamic testing.
Failure to observe the predicted mechanical-property combination or the proposed microstructural signatures would falsify the hypothesis.
